SIMULACRA scared the absolute crap out of me, and that’s one of the biggest compliments I can give a horror game. The entire game takes place through a missing person’s phone, which creates a unique and immersive experience that feels unsettlingly realistic.

What makes SIMULACRA so effective is how believable everything feels. You’re scrolling through messages, watching videos, checking social media, and uncovering clues while trying to figure out what happened. As the story progresses, things become increasingly disturbing, and there were multiple moments that genuinely made me uncomfortable in the best possible way.

The game does an excellent job building tension and mystery, making it hard to put down once you start uncovering the truth. The live-action performances help sell the story, and the feeling that something is constantly watching or manipulating events keeps you on edge throughout the entire experience.

Overall, SIMULACRA is an amazing horror game that delivers both great scares and an engaging mystery. If you’re looking for a horror experience that feels different from the usual formula, I highly recommend it.

Rating: 9/10

A genuinely creepy and immersive horror game that had me hooked from beginning to end and scared me more than I expected.

review_text_raw:
It's been a while since I last played "Simulacra", but since I mentioned it when reviewing "Daemon_9" I felt that it was only fair to give the game it's due. 

As with the aforementioned 'dangerous dark web' title, "Simulacra" places YOU, the player, in the lead role. Not some character. YOU. The premise is a straight-forward one: You have stumbled across some young woman's phone and, in an attempt to discover the owner's identity, you search it's contents, only to discover that the fate of that young woman, may inevitably bring upon your own undoing as well. 

As one can imagine, the very premise of this game hinges on the morally dubious premise that in attempting to find this missing girl, going by the name of Anna, players are consciously violating her privacy by accessing her personal information through her unlocked mobile device. This issue of an individual's right to privacy has been a hot topic for some time now and has been the subject of whole games in of themselves. For "Simulacra", however, this is merely a starting point and one which tells a very different story, albeit one that deals with several other equally relevant issues instead. 

The game feels far more real-world in it's dramatic critique of New Media cultures than that of "Daemon_9", exploring the far more domestic world of mobile device apps and how they can be abused by the wrong kinds of people. Essentially, the digital paper trail that players are encouraged to follow inevitably leads them into the moral grey area of dating apps and 'hook-up' culture, where along with Anna's ex-boyfriend and a somewhat dubious acquaintance of hers, they are drawn further and further into a world that is custom-gear for self-destruction through the distortion of regular human interaction. A common theme in all of these techno-phobic gaming narratives is the belief that they lead to isolation and inevitably the erasure of physical identity by way of hikikomori (feel free to Google search that word if you want to know what it means). "Simulacra" expands this idea to quite a heavy degree, causing players to interact with all manner of "influencers" and shady individuals in order to finally come face-to-face with the kidnapper.   

The trouble with this game in comparison to "Daemon_9" is that while both games involve re-playing old footage and analysing information, "Simulacra" feels like a far more passive gaming experience. Whereas the former game has characters glaring down the barrel of the camera at you, in this instance the game instead tries to maintain at least some degree of a fourth wall. Considering that the whole "Simulacra" experience concerns thrusting the player into the spotlight, this can cheapen the experience with how the player becomes immersed in the experience. Though they are facing the camera front on, actors often look off-camera when performing lines which makes it feel more like a dramatically acted close-up shot to another fictional character than a direct address to the player. Don't get me wrong. The young cast fair very well with the material that they are given and all give admirable performances. It just feels like they were being asked to treat the video sequences more like a piece of scripted drama by the director instead of recreating a piece of Vlog or V-phone footage. When all is said and done, such methods do make the overall experience a little lack-lustre given that one unnecessary degree of separation.  

More promising, however, are the dialogue phases which are conducted through SMS sequences. Here the immersion process is far more convincing, due in no small part to the fact that players are actively engaging with the drama instead of simply receiving video/audio information. The presentation of these sequences also mean that they are not hindered by the usual Stop/Start mechanics to which conversational dialogue phases are usually tied, thus making it feel more natural and organic. This immersion also helps create a sense of helplessness when control is periodically wrested away from the player in a conscious nod to the modern surge of remote hacking and cyber attacks. 

In summary, I do highly recommend "Simulacra" because it is a very good premise for a game. As Major Kusanagi famously said in the conclusion to Mamoru Oshii's "Ghost In The Shell": "The Net is vast and infinite", and as the digital landscape continues to expand the possibilities for new narrative material surrounding new media technologies grows with it. However, as a narrative gaming experience it is a mixed bag. The social commentary aspects of this game, and of it's spin-off "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams", more than warrant at least two full play throughs. However, as far as Interactive FMV dramas go, one is better suited to buying "Her Story", "The Infectious Madness of Dr. Dekker" or the "Daemon_9".

After the success of [b]Sara Is Missing[/b], it was obvious [i]Kaigan Games[/i] would continue in the same vein of development. Truth is, before [b]Sara is Missing[/b], there was [b]Finding Home[/b], an indie game also simulating a smartphone experience. Seems the studio entire direction is surrounded by this peculiar genre, one that connects players into a stylized voyeur adventure never seen before.

In [b]SIMULACRA[/b] players gain access to a smartphone belonging to a young woman named Anna. She’s just like any other girl in her early 20’s, working and having a good time with her friends online and offline. All seems perfectly fine, except Anna went missing and she left a strange, bizarre video, as her last registered action.

The overall story is embedded within Anna’s online actions, and each new lead will reveal parts of her past, with phone backups and confessions from her friends. Dialogues are pretty realistic and interesting, making the overall experience more pleasant. There’s no drama, but it’s still somehow intense with a touch of horror and matching jump scares.

Players will explore Anna’s inner secrets and sneak peek into her life, as well as in her problems. Through smartphone apps, such as email, chats, and even the equivalent of Twitter and Tinder, we’ll meet her acquaintances and find clues that may lead to Anna’s whereabouts. While browsing text and pictures, we can restore them by either forming a phrase out of loose words, and building an image by restoring little pieces at a time.

Finding Anna is as much part of the story, as create a connection with other persons of interest through social media. You’ll have to find clues and discover ways to connect with others, to collect new information. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] allows you to open up, or, in some cases, keep pretending to be Anna, which may open up new dialogue options and information.

There’s a certain acquired taste when going through someone else’s life, and the game clearly explores that with decency, but still waving a round or two of peculiar situations and encounters. Some internet references and expressions can be found all over the place, adding a certain style and characterization of realism into that social media life.

It’s one of those experiences, where you’ll forget you’re in the game. As soon as the clues start rolling down and the story involving, it’s a fantastic journey. Gathering clues and finding the direction to go was always relatively easy, and I never found myself stuck or without an idea of where to go. The game also contains a section with the objectives, which will help out in most scenarios if needed.

The visual presentation is accurate and suiting. It’s far more comfortable browsing this virtual phone, then rather use a phone in real life obviously, since the game grants resolutions up to your own. Videos and pictures follow the expected quality and it’s an authentic experience as far as design goes.

Indie games featuring live-action performances with quality are rare. Most of the times the studio goes to an alternative or stylized acting. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] though, doesn’t need any of those tricks, and [url=www.instagram.com/wendyvanhoren/]Wendy Van Horen[/url] plays Anna surprisingly well. Some may claim it’s an amateurish act, but remember, this is Anna’s life, a young person sharing vlogs about her personal life experiences. Wendy definitely brings the character alive, adding a natural and realistic touch.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] dwells between our presence in the real world, versus our digital personas. I personally think it’s a really good concept and it’s well depict. Doesn’t become far-fetched, even when dealing with the supernatural. It’s a horror experience, but more towards what social media means to us, and how scary it can become. Very entertaining and for the simple price of $3,99 it’s impossible to avoid recommending this one.

Sad to say that I had to refund this. The premise seemed solid based on the store page - trying to piece together clues to someone's disappearance when you only have their phone - and the general interface was well done, but that was about it. My first hour of playing this mostly consisted of:

[list]
[*] Listening to overdramatic, very slowly worded voice messages.
[*] Piecing together "corrupted" pictures and texts that had absolutely nothing to do with Anna's disappearance. 
[*] Wondering if a proofreader was ever used for this game. Most of the articles and texts gave me the impression that English isn't the developer's first language. While I have nothing against that, coming across awkward grammar really took the immersion out of a mostly text-based game.
[*] Sitting through consecutive rounds of text-vomit finger-pointing from Greg and Taylor. I truly detest people who text at a rate of 50 messages/min when a single sentence would have sufficed. I didn't think it could get any worse, but in came the relationship drama...
[*] An overall disconnect between the gameplay and the plot. A girl disappears with clear hints of some non-human entity behind it, so why am I wasting my time investigating the sorry backgrounds of two garden-variety losers?
[/list]

Maybe the game gets better beyond the 1.7-hour point, but I really didn't have the patience to sit through constant notifications from the Male MC Idiot Express while waiting for some actual horror story to happen. Honestly, I'd have been happier to just shut the damn phone off and actually set out to find Anna door to door. At least then the "investigation" would have felt more productive.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra wasn't an entirely bad experience. I actually had a decent time with most of the game. However, the overall package is important to me with a game. I only played through Mass Effect 3 once because the endings were so off-putting that I did not have any interest in playing through again because the conclusion lowered the quality of the game as a whole for me. Mind you, Simulacra doesn't have two games that came before it to ruin the legacy of or anything, nor is it even a tenth the length of Mass Effect 3, but an unsatisfying conclusion to any heavily story-focused game is often the ruin of many a game that were doing well up until that point.

With Simulacra, you navigate a missing girl's cell phone, using the text messaging, web browser, social media posts, and a dating app to further your investigation into where the girl is, gain a couple of allies to help with said investigation, and ultimately conclude with a villain which I won't spoil the identity of or anything like that. I will say that you should be able to easily understand a great villain when the villain monologues to you about why said villain is doing things, and there should be some logical explanations for the reasoning for the villain's actions, etc. Also, a villain shouldn't just pop out of nowhere, typically. Imagine if you got to the end of a deep storyline, and suddenly an extraterrestrial pops out without proper foreshadowing. It would make for a "good bad movie," but a terrible plot point. Again, I won't say specifics about this villain, but the villain does not seem to have a very logical viewpoint, and the villain pops practically out of nowhere and can do things that the game never explains which are vital to the main storyline.

Finally, there appear to be four different endings. Apparently the game locks you out of certain endings based on certain actions you take at some point in the game. I have no idea what those actions were or when they came up. Worse yet, there is no manual saving in Simulacra. There is ONE autosave file that overwrites every time you complete an objective, meaning to see the other endings, you have to start the game from the beginning again. The text messages pop up faster than before, but the game still takes too long for me to have the patience to play through it again, especially since the gameplay wasn't particularly enjoyable for me. Simulating a real cell phone was a cool premise, but it wasn't "fun" to interact with for me outside of the initial surprises of what the very small cast of characters (and an even smaller cast of *relevant* characters) have to say.

The ending I got was horribly dark and unpleasant, and the other ending that was offered to me was clearly going to be horribly dark and unpleasant as well. Dark endings can be entertaining if the storyline gives a satisfying quality to them that doesn't leave you feeling cheated. In Simulacra, the villain effectively tells you "lulz, you made decisions (that I'm not going to specify which ones or when) which set this stuff up. Now make horrible choice A, or horrible choice B." I stopped caring about the story immediately upon being given these options, and just proceeded to the ending knowing my conclusion was going to suck because I didn't play with a walkthrough and the game doesn't allow saving aside from the regularly-overwriting autosave, so you can't just load back a few minutes to make a different decision and see things play out differently.

Without very clear points of making relevant decisions, and without a manual save you can load, AND without enjoyable dark/"bad" endings, Simulacra left me disappointed in what initially seemed like a game I was going to talk about to others and say great things about it, but walling off endings sneakily and overwriting autosaves without a manual save option ruined the overall package of this game for me. I already regret the time I spent on it and I'm not going to waste any more of my time looking up the other endings online or replaying it. I will forever remember the crap ending choice the game locked me into and look back on Simulacra with disdain and disappointment.

I already own the sequel, Simulacra 2, but I no longer intend to play it because I dislike the first game so much now.

!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. I understand their intention was to heighten the atmosphere of fear, but with the quality of the storytelling, I'm not sure that any additional atmosphere was really needed. Instead of shocking me, the rare jump scare attempts and 'spooky imagery' instead removed me from the story, and reminded me that I was, in fact, completely safe in my computer chair, instead of inside a strange house looming over a stranger's phone. Like the minigames, though, the attempted jump scares are sparsely placed within the game, and didn't detract from my overall enjoyment.

The total of my playtime consists of a single playthrough of the game, so use that as a measuring stick for how long a standard run will last. Despite enjoying the game very much, I do not think I'll replay it, mostly because I don't have a completionist mentality, and I was very satisfied from a single playthrough, but I definitely intend to do some research on what my decisions could have changed. If you're in the mood for a quick, but good story with compelling characters and a great design, than I'd highly recommend Simulacra. 

Thanks to the development team! You can tell a lot of love went into this game, and it was so much fun to play!

[h2] Simulacra Review: A Promising Start That Loses Its Way [/h2]

Simulacra is an intriguing, story-driven game that draws players in with its early mystery and atmosphere. However, as the game progresses, it begins to lose momentum, culminating in an abrupt and unsatisfying ending. Despite this, the game is still worth experiencing for those who enjoy narrative-focused titles, though it has a few notable shortcomings.

[h3] The Good: [/h3]

1) Compelling Start: From the beginning, Simulacra presents an engaging and mysterious premise that immediately captures the player's attention. The game’s atmosphere and pacing set the stage for an intriguing narrative.

2) Satisfying Puzzle Solving: For those with a keen eye for detail, solving the puzzles is rewarding. The game often challenges players to analyze small clues, and the sense of satisfaction upon uncovering key pieces of the story is one of its standout features.

3) Impactful Choices: The game does well in giving players the feeling that their choices matter. How you respond to certain characters affects their relationships with you, adding a layer of depth and emotional investment to the experience.

[h3] The Bad: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Gameplay: Unfortunately, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive as the game progresses. The entire experience is confined to a phone screen, and while this fits the premise, it can become tiresome over time, as the game rarely deviates from this formula.

2) Lack of Explanation for the Antagonist: The game’s main antagonist remains cryptic, with little explanation given for their motivations or origins. This leaves players with more questions than answers, which can feel frustrating for those who prefer a clear narrative.

3) Abrupt Ending: One of the biggest letdowns is the ending. For a story-based game, the conclusion should feel like a natural payoff, but instead, it feels rushed and unfinished, leaving many of the game’s intriguing threads unresolved. The game’s narrative feels carried more by its strong start than by its finale.

[h3] The Ugly: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Playthroughs: Replaying the game is a tedious process as players must start from scratch. There is no checkpoint system to revisit critical moments or alter the story’s outcome without going through the entire experience again. This makes multiple playthroughs feel like a chore.

2) Frustrating Achievements: Some of the achievements are either too obscure or require an unreasonable amount of time and patience to unlock. This might be off-putting for those who are not inclined to consult a guide or spend excessive hours grinding.

3) Annoying Sound Effects: While the sound design in Simulacra is generally effective, the game occasionally relies on loud, jarring noises in an attempt to startle the player. These moments feel cheap and detract from the otherwise immersive experience, disrupting the atmosphere rather than enhancing it.

[h3] Conclusion: 6/10 [/h3]

Simulacra has a lot to offer in terms of its mystery and narrative, especially for those who enjoy story-driven experiences. However, the lack of a satisfying ending, repetitive gameplay, and the absence of convenience features like a checkpoint system hold it back from being a truly great game. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re a fan of mystery and story-focused titles, but if you’re sensitive to flashing lights or sudden loud noises, it might be best to approach with caution.

review_text_raw:
[b]Simulacra[/b] is a "found phone" game—a genre where players uncover clues after discovering a stranger's lost smartphone. While the concept has gained popularity in the last decade, games have experimented with faux interfaces mimicking imagined technology for years. I remember playing Mean Streets and the officially licensed X-Files game, both of which attempted something similar.

In Simulacra, you navigate the protagonist's phone within the game's tightly controlled framework, piecing together what happened to its owner. I was initially drawn to the game due to the resurgence of modern full-motion video (FMV) storytelling. Having enjoyed 2015's Her Story, I expected a similar experience. While Simulacra integrates FMV clips effectively, its "found phone" premise was far less compelling to me. I think I hit an audience mismatch—I’m simply not a fan of smartphones. Since I don't particularly enjoy using my own phone, the idea of rifling through someone else’s was unappealing. I played on my laptop and embarrassingly took about a third of the game to realize that it was undoubtedly designed to be played on a smartphone—duh.

The protagonist, Anna, feels like a generic twenty-something woman struggling with rocky relationships, an unfulfilling job, and repeated rejections in her academic and professional pursuits. [spoiler]She has a non-binary best friend, which the game seemingly frames as a revelation, but it’s so heavily telegraphed that it falls into cliché territory.[/spoiler] In fact, Anna herself is a walking cliché, as is the familiar "technology is evil" theme—an overused trope in uninspired sci-fi narratives. After seeing it so often, it no longer has much impact for me.

The game’s title did surprise me. Before playing, I had never encountered the terms "Simulacra" or "Simulacrum," which piqued my curiosity. Midway through, I looked up the meaning, wondering why a game about a woman's lost phone would have such a name. Ah, crap—spoilers.

As for gameplay, Simulacra offers little freedom. Players must follow rigidly scripted conversations in a precise order to unlock new options and clues. While there are minor choices in how you interact with Anna’s close friends, they ultimately boil down to a few dialogue changes that determine which of the five endings you get—most of which depend on choices made in the last 10% of the game. That said, I appreciated that I could make all the necessary connections without resorting to a guide or hints. That sense of progress and accomplishment is something lacking in other puzzle or adventure games.

Overall, Simulacra is predictable but not necessarily bad. The FMV clips are well-integrated, Wendy Van Horen Carneiro delivers a solid performance as the wronged damsel in distress, and the faux-phone interface is thoughtfully designed. I give it a [b]3 out of 5[/b]—though the game is clearly aimed at a different audience than me, so others may find it more engaging.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. What begins as a seemingly straightforward search quickly evolves into a dark, psychological thriller that unravels through the phone’s contents, offering an immersive narrative experience driven entirely by player interaction with texts, apps, videos, and social media. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

At its core, Simulacra excels at storytelling through environmental and digital clues, requiring players to carefully sift through Anna’s phone for evidence to understand what happened to her. The game’s interface convincingly mimics a real smartphone, complete with calls, messages, emails, and even a creepy AI assistant named "Maya" that adds an additional layer of eerie presence. Players must navigate conversations, unlock apps, and decrypt files, which gradually reveal Anna’s troubled life and the sinister forces at play. The game’s narrative pacing is well-calibrated, steadily building suspense while offering occasional moments of emotional vulnerability that make Anna’s plight feel deeply personal and urgent.

Visually, Simulacra embraces a minimalistic but effective approach, using the phone’s screen as the main canvas for its storytelling. The user interface is polished and intuitive, making it easy to become engrossed in the investigation without distractions. The game’s use of sound design is particularly noteworthy — ambient noises, notification sounds, and voice messages all contribute to the growing sense of dread. The lack of traditional cinematic cutscenes is replaced by clever interactive sequences that heighten immersion and player agency, ensuring that every discovery feels earned and impactful.

One of the standout features of Simulacra is its branching narrative and multiple endings, which encourage players to explore different paths and decisions throughout the game. This replayability factor enhances the game’s value and allows for varied emotional outcomes, depending on the player’s choices. The writing is generally sharp, weaving together elements of horror, thriller, and drama while avoiding common genre clichés. The characters, though primarily seen through their digital personas, are well fleshed out, and the voice acting adds authenticity to the conversations, heightening the emotional stakes.

That said, Simulacra is not without its limitations. Some players might find the pacing slow during certain investigative segments, and the reliance on reading through extensive text may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for more action-oriented gameplay. Additionally, the horror elements are more psychological and subtle rather than jump-scare-heavy, which might not satisfy fans expecting traditional scares. Technical issues, such as occasional app glitches or interface bugs, have also been reported but generally do not detract significantly from the overall experience.

Overall, Simulacra stands out as a unique and compelling title that pushes the boundaries of interactive horror by situating its narrative within the intimate space of a smartphone. Its creative storytelling approach, immersive sound design, and chilling atmosphere combine to deliver an experience that feels both modern and unsettling. For players who appreciate mystery, psychological horror, and narrative-driven games that challenge them to piece together a story from fragmented clues, Simulacra offers a memorable journey into the dark side of digital life and human vulnerability.

Rating: 9/10

review_text_raw:
If you have ever wondered how ugly it could get in the event that AI were to take over, well, this game depicts one possible reality. 

Enjoyed it overall, but aiming to reach 100% completion left me with mixed feelings.


Simulacra is a modern take on a philosophical idea that originated in an essay called "Simulacra and Simulation" from 1981. It's simple, and yet, if you manage to reach any ending, and the true ending especially, you will likely ask yourself questions about how you approach your existence in our digitalised world.

The game has its flaws, but if you're okay with this format, then you will probably have a good time.


When I played Simulacra for the first time in 2018, I played it, and I enjoyed it a lot. I was impressed by the simplistic yet effective nature of the storytelling that was made relevant due to the then technologically transitional period: everyone learning how to use smartphones for almost anything. I also appreciated how little the game requires of you, safe for the patience to read, comprehend, observe, and stop to think for a moment, making it an easy recommendation for playing after a mentally and physically demanding day.

That was then. But what about now...?


Lately, I had been thinking a lot about the topics of Simulacra, Simulation, Simulacrum, and AI, so I decided to replay the game and complete it because I liked it so much my first time. It took me 2 playthroughs to reach completion. The first one took 4-5 hours, and the second - no more than 2-3. My recommendation if you were to seek completion within the day would be to do it with a guide next to you. Some achievements, especially the hidden one and the true ending, require noticing and doing a number of things, which could take you hours to nail by going back again and again -- which could be enjoyable if you're into that and are okay with spending more time with the game.

And here is a thing you'll wish to keep in mind: to reach 100% completion, you will need to open the corresponding save file folder, and create multiple backups (ideally, giving yourself context because it gets hard to make out the saves), because you will need to go back if you don't want to replay the game 5 or 6 times. Most of all, the save files will help you in the event that the game bugs out, as it tends to do -- for instance, when you use your keyboard to input something, and then press Enter, the game crashes; for others, some chats don't load properly; for others yet, some achievements refuse to pop up on the first or second try; and so on.


Do your due diligence to find out what's needed for 100% completion. I used Naps' guide on PlayStationTrophies.org, and made plenty of back up saves along the way. Feel free to comment if you need the files for your run, though imo it's more fun to do it along the way.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a game about something. I'm not really sure what, since the game is practically foreshadowing its own inability to deliver on its buildup in many places, and the solution to the mystery had me wondering why there even was a mystery to solve, being that it was something which had little to do with anything that exists in the real world (though there is doubtless some deep philosophical meaning behind the Ghost of Facebook Profiles Past throwing someone off a building for not having enough followers on MySpace).
The story is told through a cast of characters, inlcuding, but not limited to: A man who you can convince to commit corporate espionage and B&E in one sentence each, a sex offender who couldn't shut up to save his life, and the girl who went missing, has her entire character arc revealed in chapter one and never gets any more developement aside from us finding out that everything she did was, in fact, understandable, if rude. All of these reserved seats on the short bus are caught up in a missing person case, but have to do it through the player character, who has his own character, and who can't count to his own IQ. The story is told through tweedle dee and tweedle dum figuring out ways to get more evidence, and the protagonist actually doing it.
The dialogue system is both good and bad. It's bad because the dialogue was bootlegged from Fallout 4, and rarely had the thing I wanted to say, and good in that they actaully manage to do more with it than Bethesda ever did. As stated, the two stooges figure out new ways to attack the case and figure things out, and you actaully do it with puzzling that ranges from "good" to "really bad". There are puzzles where you put together images such that htere's no corruption, which I liked,  puzzles where you unscramble sentences, which were rarely necessary but also rarely obnoxious, and there were puzzles where you have an article to draw information from, but the information in the article is more wrong than the information Bill Cosby the 2nd pulls out of thin air.
Don't worry about the horror elements, it's just a few loud noises and distorted images. So we have a game where the horror is token, the story is confusing, and the characters are dumb and/or pricks. It's technically perfectly adequate, but so are virtually all visual novels, and what extra this does amounts to set decoration. 3/10, since someone who is willing to not think too hard might find it artistically brilliant.

I must admit. I really REALLY enjoyed playing this game.

When I first saw the tag 'Horror', I was a little scared to play this. I'm not a fan of things that scare me, but I managed to get through this and had a blast. *There are a couple jumpscares obviously because why not XD* (I legit flip out at them and tell them to screw off haha)

So in short, Simulacra is about a girl named Anna who has gone missing, and you have to dig through information through her apps, photos, friends, and even people outside of her circle, in order to find out what the hell happened to her.

And I mean you have to dig through a lot of information sometimes.

However, it's not to say that it wasn't fun doing a treasure hunt. Whenever I figured out how to solve one of the tasks based on the information found in different apps, I felt overjoyed. This game makes you really look for the clues where it makes sense.

Also, by the end of the game, I almost felt like I knew the characters. They were very believable, and that's what really connected with me.

Overall, I just love the idea of using solely a phone. It creates a constraint, allowing for so many possibilities and new ways to create and solve puzzles.

I can say that I have only a couple complaints though.

1) When you look through Anna's message history, you come upon these special messages that are in complete disarray. In order to understand what it said, you had to rearrange the words to fix the message. Sometimes, it was just really difficult for me to figure out what that sentence was. I sometimes maybe spent a little too much time and couldn't progress until I figured it out. Most of the messages weren't important enough to do this, except for one. To be honest, I'm probably just not very good at it.

I only really decrypted those messages for my own curiosity, but because they weren't extremely important except for the story-important ones, there was no huge incentive to decode them.

2) While I do like treasure hunting for those sweet juicy clues in the phone data, sometimes the hints are a little too subtle. I'm not extremely great at puzzle games, so I'll miss details, whether they are obvious or not. I think I took a break because I spent so much time trying to figure out something that was so obvious because I simply missed the detail in a sea of texts. Not a big issue, but I just wanted to point that out for the average gamer playing this. I mean I had to look up something once, so it's not bad on my end.

All in all, this game was just amazing, and I look forward to see what's next :D

(Seriously though. I recommend playing this without any spoilers. This was an amazing experience, and it was a good price for such a wonderful story)

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is another game within the sara is missing universe. The first game was good but with new additions to a series brings new mechanics and fixes the short commings of the original, does this game do just that? I will be reviewing the game with a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The game is very creepy. Now jumpscares are cheap and something I dont really enjoy but the game has ambient sound effects that are very spooky. Sometimes you may hear nocking at a door or a wisper or see the lights flicker in your field of view. Some are not really strong in spooking the player but the sound effects really sell the horror.

      The plot is good. Now this is pretty much a horror thriller game that delves with a deep mystery. The game throws you for many loops making you question who can you trust and how much information you should provide. You never know who is at the other end of that text message you recieved. The further you go the deeper the rabbit hole goes.

        The gameplay is simplistic. A game having a simplistic gameplay is nothing to fear. This is like playing a tale tell game where you get dialogue options but sometimes it effects the response of other players and the ending. There are branching paths but not many to get more than 2ish playthroughs. Still it is good to see that some choices creates a response that effect the story and feels a bit like a genuine response in a hypothetical world.

Con:
      There are some puzzles that are difficult. This game has quite a few moments that test memory and makes you search for clues to progress but some of these clues are very well hidden meaning in order to progress you might need to search the internet for the solution to save the frustration. It is a minor issue but i swear there is this one puzzle i could never solve.

Conclusion:
       In short this game is short but it is a blast to play. The story is creepy with atmoshere and has a great story. If you play the game for just a short ammount of time you will be hooked into finding out the truth. I can not reccomend this game enough for anything curious in the game. It is resonably priced in retrospect to how long the game is.

review_text_raw:
I enjoy these 'immersive sim' games where you look through devices for clues to a mystery like A Normal Lost Phone or even Hypnospace Outlaw. I liked trawling through old messages and finding tidbits of information that would help me solve a mystery or hack into a passworded account to find more clues. 

I thought that Simulacra would be similar to those kinds of games, but maybe with a more harrowing twist as it's labelled as 'horror'. However I found there to be minimal 'puzzle' elements here, and any that did exist were fairly obvious to figure out. Instead the game is pushed forward by the other characters in the game, who clearly tell you what to do next at each stage.

So the focus of the game is mainly on the story, which I felt was pretty weak. The characters kept railroading me into doing things I didn't want to, like investigating a topic I didn't think had merit, or making me give information to somebody I didn't trust in order to push the plot forward. I thought the final reveal was bizarre and the 'villain's' motives were contrived. It seemed like the devs were trying to send some fancy message about society but hadn't done a good enough job of fleshing it out throughout the game so it all just felt flat at the end.

Several of the other reviews describe the tone of the plot as 'goofy', which I think is fitting but weird for a so-called horror game. Unfortunately the horror aspects solely comes from the occasional jump scare where an image pop ups with a scream, like the prank videos people used to send each other....

And lastly, there are 4 different endings, but getting them is really unsatisfying. To get the best ending, you have to constantly lie to people even if there is seemingly no reason to do so. The middle endings rely on you going out of your way to befriend a random stranger during a potential kidnapping, despite the game giving you many reasons to suspect them. Most people will choose to remain suspicious of every potential suspect but still not lie to anyone, and get the bad ending which makes all your work a waste of time.

My first experience with the found phone game genre was disappointing. I found [I]Replica[/I] to be an undercooked, preachy, borderline sciolistic game that is best not played. My excitement for this genre was quashed quickly, but I remembered that I still have [I]SIMULACRA[/I] in my backlog of games. Because of that, I decided to give found phone games another try.

Coincidentally, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] was partly inspired by [I]Replica[/I] (as seen by the titles), and partly by [I]Her Story[/I], one of my favourite games of all time. I loved [I]Her Story[/I] for its intriguing narrative and presentation, so I had some hope for [I]SIMULACRA[/I]. Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint.

[I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable.

Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary.  Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian.

As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me.

P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? I think not!), and [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is clearly more refined in both story and game mechanics. Both games are worth playing, as they are both good ambassadors for the found phone game genre.

review_text_raw:
Love this game. In the same vein as films like 'Searching', you spend all of your time navigating a device (in this case a phone) in search of a missing person. Simulacra has more a horror tone than 'Searching', but for much of the game's runtime it's only lightly scary, with most of the suspense coming not from supernatural frights but from further unraveling the mystery by feeling like an amateur cybersleuth. 

There are definitely moments where it was frustrating trying to figure out where to go next, but the game generally does a good job of pointing you in the right direction through the use of hints given by the characters in the game. It all feels organic and never too forced. Multiple playthroughs will be needed to see all of the endings, but even just one playthrough will give every player a satisfying experience in the end. 

My few gripes with this game are that the actors aren't really that great in their performances, and for a game that I think is set in the US (at least that seems like the accent everyone is going for), the actor's accents waver quite often. This is obviously not a big budget production, so it's understandable that top shelf talent isn't within reach, but I would say that instead of trying to force a setting, just go with what's available around you. I don't feel that the US setting is necessary to tell this kind of story. I'd also like if there were some way to expedite replays of the game. Yes, if you do a second playthrough you can skip text much more quickly, but I'm thinking of something kinda like Zero Escape: Virtue's Last Reward. In that title there was a branching path menu you could pull up and jump exactly to the point where the story diverged. That would save so much time replaying up until the point where a critical decision was made. 

Conclusion:

[h1]Final Verdict: Buy! Spoiler-Free Review.[/h1]

This game took me about 3.5 hours to complete on my first playthrough (there are alternate endings available). I tried to read every bit of text and watch every video / photo involved. This game does disappoint as a horror game, but as a mystery thriller, it is excellent. 

This is not a mixed or alternate reality game where you search the web for answers or give your e-mail. The experience is pretty linear, although you can make different choices, the experience goes pretty much through the same set of main events (except for the endings which can vary). You will be looking through videos, photos, Jabbr (facebook), Spark (Tinder), the web (in-game only browser), phone numbers, and e-mails. You simply have to find the relevant information to unlock passcodes or find connections to progress the story. 

You will also have dialogue choices. Some of those choices can have an impact on the story, for example, having more trust with that person and thus giving you a different ending. The story starts out very strong when it is a mystery about what happened to the missing woman, Anna. Even the creepy stuff is exciting at first when you see the distorted videos and the atmosphere leaves things to the imagination. The dialogue between characters is well-written. 

Unfortunately, when you find out the mystery then the horror elements become more silly than scary. I actually just started to troll everybody, trying to get the worst possible ending. There was some real tension at the start and middle of this game, but towards the end, I really didn't feel any connection to any of the characters or "the danger" involved.

That's a shame because this is a very polished experience. The actors all did a nice job overall (sure some of the acting could have been better, but it's better than what is in most games). The mystery sequences where you're sleuthing and trying to find the truth all work extremely well. It's just too bad it ends in a whimper instead of a bang.

[b]Rate 7/10. I still recommend this. With a better ending(s), this could have been something very special. Good overall, but should have been great![/b]

A decent enough experience!
The story revolves around the player who receives a phone by a missing girl by the name of Anna and you  must figure out where she went missing and save her while also figuring out about what is causing the many disappearances that have been happening on a dating app. The characters in this game are really cringy and can be hard to enjoy or even have a connection with. The story itself is alright as it does help carry the game along, but its nothing special. 
There really isn't a setting as it takes place all on a phone but its a pretty unique scenario for the player to be put in.

The gameplay is fairly simple as all you do is either select different dialog choices, do mini puzzles to load back information and finding clues to move on in the story. Gameplay is decent enough as the story that it intertwines with help it feel more satisfying to do. Finally, i do like the fact that there are multiple endings and outcomes that you experience through the game which would give it more replay-ability
Overall, Simulacra does has a few flaws but if you looking for a decent, unique experience to kill a few hours with i would definitely recommend this.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is essentially a found footage film but as a game.
One day someone leaves you a phone at your doorstep, which belongs to a girl that has gone missing.
From there, it's your job to snoop through her phone to uncover hints on what happened to her.
The actors can be very cheesy and hardly believable, but that has it's own charm if you are into that kind of thing. The problem I had with the story was the horror elements that they try to shove in, in the form of jump scares. Apart from being the annoying type of jump scares, they also immediately take the story in a direction, where you as the player know where the story will end up. If the jump scares where replaced with more subtle hints that something is off, I think it would have been a lot more engaging.
  
To give credit to the devs, they did a good job at imitating a phone OS with  multiple apps. That makes it fun to snoop around for clues on how to gain access to specific parts of the phone. Even though you have a variety of apps to explore, however, multitasking is something that the fake OS lacks, which makes jumping back and forth from different apps a chore. Having to constantly scroll through everything to get to the part you need can quickly become a nuisance, especially when it deletes the things you have to fill in.

Despite these issues, I still enjoyed the game enough to recommend it for the price. It only takes around 3 to 4 hours to finish, but it has multiple endings. A new game plus mode exists, which fast-forwards the conversations. I wish it would skip the puzzles as well, so you can just focus on the endings, but alas, it is what it is.

review_text_raw:
8/10

A very interesting and well done horror game about fiddling with a stranger's phone.

Before Simulacra, the devs made Sara is Missing, a game following the same line (horror game about exploring someone's phone) and, in Simulacra, it's easy to notice how much the game has evolved. While in SIM there were some choices to be made but ultimately they didn't change all that much, in the case of Simulacra it actually changes, with 4 possible different endings depending on what you do during the game.

The game involves talking to people using the phone's messenger app, browsing through other apps, searching for clues and solving some puzzles, while experiencing some creepy things on the way. The story, although somewhat linear (with some differences based on your choices) is interesting and well done. Beating the game once also allows the player to start a new game with faster text speed, which allows for faster playing in order to obtain the different endings.

I think the only two things I feel the game could have done better is that, first, it could have been a little more creepy. Not that it's not creepy - it certainly is - but it's also a little predictable. It could have had some less predictable moments like [spoiler]weird messages showing up in the middle of normal conversations, creepy pictures/videos opening out of nowhere, etc[/spoiler]. The second thing being that there are a few conversations (not many however - just a few) that go on for longer than they need to, sidetracking into subjects that aren't ultimately important when you're trying to find a missing person.

Nonetheless, a very good game and easily worth its asking price.

Also, for anyone who likes this game, I'd also suggest the free game they have released also from the Simulacra series, called "Simulacra: Pipe Dreams".

Simulacra is a "found phone" psychological mystery / horror game where your curiosity has gotten you involved with a mystery... You found this phone on your doorstep. You initially have no idea what to enter, then the phone glitched and revealed its passcode. You find chat logs, call logs, and the owner was Anna. There was a corrupted video where a terrified Anna screamed that don't come after her... Then the message was cut off. 

As you scan the phone's various steps for clues, and maybe even engage in some social engineering with Anna's friends, including (ex-?) boyfriend Greg, bestie Ashley, and dating app date Taylor, you need to reconstruct Anna's life before she went missing, to have a chance at finding out what happened to her...  

The videos are very high quality, but the simulated phone calls don't sound nearly as good. 

The special effects where the phone glitched got the definitely horror feel to it. Same with the time-warp feel when the phone really glitches out. 

The puzzles such as the sentence scramble and photo scramble doesn't quite fit into the gameplay though.  The "sentence scramble" feels a bit of "make work". Same with the photo scramble. 

There seems to be a lot of alternative paths one can take, so there would be a lot of additional achievements should you want a replay or two. 

All puzzles have clues accessible within the phone itself, though some may be more obscure than others. Part of the fun is to figure out the rest. And there are a lot of red herrings. 

All in all, interesting mechanic for a puzzle game and gradual revelation, if you dig this sort of game.

I got this game today and I was incredibly excited to play. I did around 4 playthroughs, trying to see the easter eggs and gather all the achievements and overall I'm rather amazed.

The use of real people in a game was a new concept to me but I enjoyed the idea a lot, especially since it highlighted the possible dangers of the digital world and made them more transferrable to the real world. The voice acting was a bit unrealistic sometimes but that's a minor issue. 

There are 5 possible endings (though the game at the end shows you only four of them) and your choices really impact them. The dialogue options that the game revolves around either make or break your case, so you have to think about what to choose.

The game is rather easy, in most cases if you get stuck at anything either of the two characters that you keep talking to will help you. 

After over 6 hours of playthrough, I have to say I am really impressed with this game. It was my first time ever playing something of this format and I will now have expectations for the future. I would not count this game as a horror, since the repeated jumpscares and glitches were far from scary (but maybe they might scare some people, who knows!). The true scary theme in the game is the realization that people on the Internet might really be bad and you shouldn't trust everyone you meet online. 

Even though it's common knowledge, when showcased like this, it can be eye-opening to some. Great game.

Even though it's common knowledge, when showcased like this, it can be eye-opening to some. Great game.

TLDR: Cute little horror game with lots of jump scares and some bad acting. Social media in this game was amazing fun. Pick it up on sale.

An adventure horror game all happening in somebody's phone. You essentially play as yourself, trying to solve the mystery of the phone's owner's disappearance with the help of her friends. The puzzles are not very difficult, but engaging enough to keep you hooked in the story. There were some really spooky segments so I'd recommend playing this in a dark quiet room to get its full potential.

The story was fun, reasonably short. Editing Anna's social media was definitely the biggest highlight of my playthrough - you get absolute freedom in Anna's phone. Devs could only make this better by adding more consequences to it. You will spend a lot of time talking to 2 of the biggest cringelords in games everywhere. Their strange behavior was topped off by their atrocious acting. Female acting was alright. There are multiple endings to reflect your choices.

All in all, I recommend getting this one on sale. It's not the best or most memorable game ever, but it's still fairly entertaining..

review_text_raw:
If you like eerie, cerebral horror, I highly recommend Simulacra, especially in a bundle with its sequel.  Things you get: 
* A new kind of evil
* Choices that matter (multiple endings)
* A very believable phone to snoop through.   The photos and other clues all blend extremely well with what you'd expect out of a typical phone. 
* Puzzles to solve, with clues often embedded into the content in ways that are not painfully obvious
* Identity theft for a good cause. 
* Both likable and unlikable characters

The only downsides here are that some of the acting quality is kind of meh, but it's an indie game, Play at night with the lights off.  This is a suspense-thriller, not a jumpscare horror-fest, so while there are a few "gotcha" moments, it is the subtle creepy stuff that will get to you.  Best played without "scouting" the plot online first; the villain reveal is much more interesting this way. 

There is also a Free to Play demisequel called Simulacra: Pipe Dreams, so if you're going for the complete collection, you need this, Simulacra 2, and Pipe Dreams.

review_text_raw:
A short and cheap game that provides a good afternoon's worth of gameplay for your first playthrough. 

The gameplay is well polished and smooth. The music is sometimes a bit too loud for my tastes but it is not bad. The smartphone interface however is very well made and simulates a more comfortable experience swiping and clicking. 

The plot is predictable and voice acting is a bit poor. But the game is rich in story-telling, whether it is relevant to the main questline or not. There is plenty of content lying around that gives the characters life and personality. While the main story is quite linear, many parts of the game can be revealed in a non-linear fashion. The attention to detail in everything in the phone is rather amazing.

The conversation choices are quite interesting and relatable, but sometimes you are forced into conversations that you don't really want to to continue for the sake of plot advancement. 

Overall a very good game well worth more than its full asking price. Will try again.
